content: Butyric acid, also known as butanoic acid, is a carboxylic acid with the chemical formula CH3CH2CH2-COOH. Its name is derived from the Greek word βούτυρος, meaning butter. This compound is present in rancid butter, Parmesan cheese, vomit, and body odor. It has a distinctly unpleasant smell and an acrid taste, though it leaves a slightly sweet aftertaste reminiscent of ether. Mammals with highly sensitive olfactory systems, such as dogs, can detect butyric acid at concentrations as low as 10 parts per billion (ppb), whereas humans typically detect it at concentrations above 10 parts per million (ppm). Butyric acid is a short-chain fatty acid that naturally occurs in the form of esters in both animal fats and plant oils. In butter, the glyceride of butyric acid constitutes approximately 3% to 4% of its composition. When butter becomes rancid, hydrolysis liberates butyric acid from its glyceride, resulting in the characteristic unpleasant odor. This compound is a significant member of the short-chain fatty acid subgroup, which shares a common -CH2COOH terminal structure, contributing to their similar chemical properties. Butyric acid is also found as hexyl butanoate in the oil of Heracleum giganteum (a type of cow parsnip) and as octyl butanoate in parsnip (Pastinaca sativa). It has been identified in bodily fluids, including sweat. Industrially, butyric acid is produced through the fermentation of sugar or starch, a process facilitated by the addition of putrefying cheese and calcium carbonate to neutralize the acids formed. The fermentation of starch can be further enhanced by introducing Bacillus subtilis. The salts and esters of butyric acid are referred to as butanoates. Butyric acid is utilized in the synthesis of various butanoate esters, many of which, such as methyl butanoate, possess pleasant aromas or flavors, making them valuable as additives in food and perfumes. These esters are also employed in organic chemistry education to demonstrate the Fischer esterification reaction. Butyric acid is an oily, colorless liquid that solidifies at -8°C and boils at 164°C. It is highly soluble in water, ethanol, and ether. When calcium chloride is added to its aqueous solution, butyric acid precipitates out. Oxidation of butyric acid with potassium dichromate and sulfuric acid yields carbon dioxide and acetic acid, while alkaline potassium permanganate oxidizes it to carbon dioxide. The calcium salt of butyric acid, Ca(C4H7O2)2·H2O, exhibits lower solubility in hot water compared to cold water. Butyric acid has a structural isomer known as isobutyric acid (2-methylpropanoic acid). Butanoate Fermentation Butanoate is produced as the end product of a fermentation process exclusively carried out by obligate anaerobic bacteria. Fermented kombucha tea contains butyric acid as a result of this fermentation. This pathway was first discovered by Louis Pasteur in 1861. Examples of butanoate-producing bacterial species include Clostridium acetobutylicum, Clostridium butyricum, Clostridium kluyveri, Clostridium pasteurianum, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens, and Eubacterium limosum. The fermentation process begins with the glycolytic breakdown of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate, as occurs in most organisms. Pyruvate is then oxidized into acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) via a unique enzymatic mechanism involving pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase. This reaction produces two molecules of carbon dioxide (CO2) and two molecules of hydrogen gas (H2) as waste products. ATP is generated in the final step of fermentation, yielding three molecules of ATP per glucose molecule, which is considered a relatively high energy yield. The balanced equation for this fermentation process is: C6H12O6 → C4H8O2 + 2CO2 + 2H2. Acetone and Butanol Fermentation Certain bacterial species can produce acetone and butanol through an alternative pathway that begins with butyrate fermentation. Examples of such species include Clostridium acetobutylicum (a prominent industrial producer of acetone and butanol), Clostridium beijerinckii, Clostridium tetanomorphum, and Clostridium aurantibutyricum. These bacteria initially follow the butanoate fermentation pathway but switch to producing butanol and acetone when the pH drops below 5. This metabolic shift helps prevent further acidification of the environment. For every molecule of acetone produced, two molecules of butanol are formed. The pathway diverges after the formation of acetoacetyl-CoA, which can either proceed to form acetone via acetoacetate or be converted into butyryl-CoA, which is subsequently reduced to butanal and then butanol. Biological Functions and Activity of Butyric Acid Highly fermentable dietary fibers, such as oat bran, pectin, and guar, are metabolized by colonic bacteria into short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate. Butanoate exhibits diverse and sometimes paradoxical effects on cellular processes such as proliferation, apoptosis, and differentiation. These effects can be either pro-neoplastic or anti-neoplastic, depending on factors such as the level of exposure, availability of other metabolic substrates, and the intracellular environment. Some studies suggest that butanoate may protect against colon cancer. However, not all research supports its chemopreventive effects, and discrepancies between in vivo and in vitro studies have led to the term butyrate paradox. Factors contributing to these inconsistent findings include differences in experimental conditions, timing and dosage of butanoate administration, dietary fiber as a confounding variable, and interactions with dietary fat. Collectively, the evidence suggests that the chemopreventive benefits of butanoate depend on factors such as the amount administered, timing relative to tumorigenesis, and the type of dietary fat consumed. Low-carbohydrate diets, such as the Atkins diet, are known to reduce butanoate production in the colon. Butyric acid is also associated with the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes, promoting a more acetylated state of histones within cells. Acetylated histones exhibit reduced affinity for DNA compared to non-acetylated histones due to the neutralization of electrostatic interactions. This modification is thought to enhance transcriptional activity at promoters that are typically silenced or downregulated by histone deacetylase activity.
